records.name: Sņežana
records.facts_used: Sņežana: The Latvian Language Agency documents Croatian Snježana rendered as Sņežana. This South Slavic family is based on snežan, snowy, from the word for snow. That explains its language history; it does not literally mean snowflake or describe a person’s appearance. The Latvian Language Agency gives the exact rendering Snježana → Sņežana, citing page 156 of a 2011 manual. This dated record illustrates transmission between languages; it is not a first birth registration or proof of one borrowing route in every family.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Exact Croatian feminine given-name agency record cites O.Bušs2011p156. No date or bridge transferred to unpalatalized or double-n forms. Exact agency HTML record https://www.personvarduatveide.lv/words/2508?locale=lv was opened; the cited printed manual page was not independently reopened unless separately noted.

records.name: Aurelija
records.facts_used: Aurelija: The Lithuanian feminine form belongs to Latin Aurelius/Aurelia, associated with aureus, golden. The colour and material word belongs to the name’s language history; it makes no claim about a bearer’s wealth or qualities. The 1964 calendar reprinted in Salys’s 1983 volume gives Aurelija (Aura) on 15 October. This is a concrete printed example of the form’s use. Its position in the historical calendar need not match every modern calendar and is not the name’s invention date.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Original Salys calendar page checked; historical printed dates differ from supplied December2. No calendar date overwritten.

records.name: Liucijus
records.facts_used: Liucijus: The name is a Lithuanian form of Latin Lucius. The family’s traditional explanation links it to lux, genitive lucis, light. That word comparison does not itself prove the story that every ancient bearer was named for birth at dawn. The 1964 calendar reprinted in Salys’s 1983 volume gives Liucijus (Liucas) on 4 March. This is a concrete printed example of the form’s use. Its position in the historical calendar need not match every modern calendar and is not the name’s invention date.
